content: Contrayerva, also known as contrajerva, refers to the root and scaly rhizome of certain tropical American species of the genus Dorstenia within the family Moraceae, specifically Dorstenia contrayerva and Dorstenia braziliensis. These plants are native to South America, and their aromatic roots have been historically utilized in medicine as mild stimulants and tonics. In earlier times, contrayerva was also employed as an antidote for snake bites. In Jamaica, the term contrayerva is used to describe a species of Birthwort, Aristolochia odoratissima, which is still believed to possess antidotal properties. The root of contrayerva is smaller than that of the iris plant, with a reddish exterior and a white interior. It is knotty and fibrous in texture. For the root to be considered effective, it must be fresh, dense, and exhibit a dusky red coloration. The odor of the root is reminiscent of fig leaves, and its taste is aromatic with a slight acrid quality. Historically, the contrayerva root was regarded by many medical writers as one of the most effective remedies for combating epidemics. Dr. Nathaniel Hodges (1629–1688), in his work on the Great Plague of London titled Loimologia (published in 1672), included a recipe in which contrayerva root was a principal ingredient. He claimed that this preparation was highly successful in treating the plague.
